worksheets.title: How Big Is a Pull? (core)

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, did the coin-pull test. She used only five-rupee coins, never a mix of coins. Why does that matter?
opts: Each five-rupee coin pulls the same amount, so every coin is the same-sized step
A mix of coins would make the notebook heavier
It does not matter at all
items.why: A unit must be the same size every time, like every centimetre on a ruler. Coins of one kind all pull about the same. A mix of big and small coins pulls by different amounts, so counting them tells you nothing. Picking 'the notebook gets heavier' mixes up the cup's pull with the notebook.

items.p: You needed 7 coins to start one notebook sliding. Guess how many coins two stacked notebooks will need. Say why you think so.
items.a: About 14 coins. Two notebooks press down on the table about twice as hard, so they grip the table about twice as much. My real result might be 13 or 15, because no test is perfectly even.
items.why: A strong answer gives a number and a reason about pressing and gripping. It also expects the real result to be close to the guess, not exactly on it.

items.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 4, needed 6 big coins to slide a notebook. His sister Meenakshi needed 12 small coins for the same notebook on the same table. Farhan says, 'Meenakshi pulled twice as hard as me.' What is wrong with his idea?
opts: It was the same pull. Only the unit was different, because her coins were smaller
Big coins always pull less than small coins
items.why: Same notebook and same table means the same pull is needed. Small coins are lighter, so more of them are needed for that pull. Farhan compared 6 and 12 without asking what each number counts. A number means nothing without its unit.

items.p: Scientists everywhere count the size of a force in ____.
items.why: Force is counted in newtons, written N for short. Everyone in the world uses the same newton, so a pull measured in Kochi can be compared with one measured in Paris.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the unit we count a force in
the tool that measures a pull
where the pointer must start, with nothing on the hook
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: The newton is the unit and the forcemeter is the tool. Mixing these two up is very common. The spring does the measuring, and the zero makes sure the measuring starts in the right place.

items.p: Look at the forcemeter. Each small mark is half a newton. How hard is it being pulled?
items.why: The pointer is on the small mark halfway between 3 and 4. Half a newton past 3 is 3 and a half newtons. Picking 3 or 4 means the small marks were not counted. Picking 35 means the 3 and the 5 were read as one number.

chart.title: A forcemeter. Each small mark is half a newton.

items.p: Divya hangs nothing on her forcemeter. Its pointer sits on 1, not on 0. What will happen if she uses it like this?
opts: Every reading will be 1 newton too big
Every reading will still be right
Every reading will be 1 newton too small
items.why: The pointer has a 1 newton head start before anything is hooked on. So every pull will show 1 newton more than it really is. That is why you check the zero first. Picking 'still right' means the zero was thought not to matter.

items.p: Ammu pushes hard on a wall, and the wall does not move. So Ammu's push was zero newtons.
items.why: False. In the balloon test, the balloon squashed most against the wall, even though the wall did not move. A force can act without making anything move. Here the wall pushed back on Ammu just as hard.

items.p: Why does a forcemeter's pointer move further for a bigger pull? Use the word spring in your answer.
items.a: Inside the forcemeter is a spring, and the pointer is fixed to it. A bigger pull stretches the spring further, so the pointer slides further down the scale.
items.why: A strong answer joins three things: the pull, the stretch of the spring, and the pointer moving with the spring. Twice the pull gives about twice the stretch.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one pull down on your hand with about 1 newton or about 10 newtons?
items.a: see items
items.why: Every 100 grams pulls down with about 1 newton. So a 100 gram thing is about 1 newton, and a 1 kilogram thing is about 10 newtons. A bar of soap is about 100 to 125 grams.

items.p: You pull a forcemeter with a sudden jerk. What does the pointer do?
opts: It jumps past the true reading for a moment
It shows the true reading straight away
items.why: A jerk makes the spring overshoot, so the pointer swings too far and then settles. That is why you pull slowly and steadily, and read the pointer only when it is still.

items.p: Put these steps for using a forcemeter in the right order.
items: check the pointer is on zero
hook on the thing and pull slowly and steadily
read the pointer with your eyes level with it
write down the number and the word newtons
items.a: order shown
items.why: Check the zero first, or every reading starts wrong. Pull steadily so the pointer does not jump. Read at eye level so the pointer does not look shifted. A number without its unit means nothing.

items.p: Many people trust their hands to tell which thing is heavier. In the big box and small box test, both boxes pulled the forcemeter to the same number. Which box felt heavier? So should we trust our hands?
items.a: Most people said the small box felt heavier, even though both pulled with the same force. Our brain expects a big box to be heavy, so it feels surprisingly light. So we cannot fully trust our hands. A forcemeter gives the same number to everyone.
items.why: A strong answer says what was felt, what the forcemeter showed, and that the two did not agree. This is called the size-weight illusion.

items.p: Kavya and her grandmother are talking about the coin-pull test.

views.says: Our coin unit is good enough. With it we can compare every notebook in our house.
Your coins are no use to your cousin in Kochi. She has different coins. Everyone should use newtons.

items.ask: Who do you agree with more? Give a reason from your coin test. Then say one good point the other person makes.
items.a: Both are partly right. Kavya is right that the coin unit works inside one house, where everyone uses the same coins. Her grandmother is right that the coin unit can't be shared with someone who has different coins. So a strong answer might say: for sharing with others, newtons are better, but for comparing at home, coins work.
items.why: A strong answer picks a side, uses something from the test (for example, 'Amma needed 12 small coins where I needed 6 big ones'), and fairly says what the other side gets right. There is no single right answer.

items.p: A small apple pulls down on your hand with about 1 newton. About how hard would a bag of 6 small apples pull?
items.why: Each apple adds about 1 newton, so 6 apples pull with about 6 newtons. Picking 60 or 600 means the newton was imagined much smaller than it is. A newton is a small force, about one apple.

items.p: Draw a forcemeter. Label the hook, the spring, the pointer and the scale. Then draw the pointer where it would be for a pull of 2 newtons.
items.a: A tube with a spring inside and a hook at the bottom. A pointer is fixed to the spring, next to a scale numbered 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on. The pointer is drawn level with the 2.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the pointer is joined to the spring, so it moves when the spring stretches. The 2 newton pointer should be further from 0 than the 1 mark.

worksheets.context: This core worksheet checks the main ideas: your own coin unit, why everyone shares the newton, and how a forcemeter works and is read.

worksheets.title: Read It, Check It (stretch)

items.p: In the water-pull activity, you started a notebook sliding with water instead of coins. Why can your cousin in Kochi repeat a water test exactly, but not a coin test?
items.a: Her coins may be different from mine, so her 'coin' would be a different size. But 100 millilitres of water is the same everywhere. Anyone with a measuring jug can pour exactly the same amount.
items.why: A strong answer says that a shared unit must be the same for everyone, and that water measured in a jug is the same in every home.

items.p: Lakshmi's forcemeter shows 1 newton with nothing on its hook. With her school bag hooked on, it shows 9 newtons. How hard does the bag really pull?
items.why: The pointer started 1 newton too far down. So take that 1 away: 9 take away 1 is 8 newtons. Picking 9 means the zero was not checked. Picking 10 means the 1 was added instead of taken away.

items.p: Thanvi wants to measure how hard a full suitcase pulls. It pulls with about 200 newtons. Which forcemeter should she use?
opts: Any of them, they all work the same
items.why: A forcemeter can only show pulls inside its range. A 200 newton pull would stretch a 0 to 10 or 0 to 50 forcemeter past its end, and could spoil the spring for good. Picking 'any of them' means the range was not thought about.

items.p: On this forcemeter, the numbers go 0, 10, 20, 30 and so on. There are 5 small gaps between each number. What does each small gap stand for?
items.why: 10 newtons shared between 5 gaps is 2 newtons for each gap. Picking 5 means the number of gaps was read as the size of each gap. Picking 10 means the big numbers and the small gaps were mixed up.

chart.title: A 0 to 50 newton forcemeter. There are 5 small gaps between each number.

items.p: On the Moon, a 1 kilogram packet of rice has less rice in it than on Earth.
items.why: False. The rice is exactly the same rice, with the same mass. Only the Moon's pull on it is smaller, about one sixth of the Earth's. A forcemeter would show less, but nothing has gone out of the packet.

items.p: Your tiffin box pulls a forcemeter down with 6 newtons on Earth. The Moon pulls about one sixth as hard. What would the forcemeter show on the Moon?
items.why: One sixth of 6 is 1. So the forcemeter would show about 1 newton. Picking 36 means multiplying by 6 instead of sharing by 6. Picking 0 means the Moon was thought to have no gravity. It does, but less.

items.p: In the bathroom scale test, the number dipped when you bent your knees quickly. Did you get lighter for a moment? What does the scale really measure?
items.a: No. My body did not lose anything. As I dropped, my feet pushed less on the scale, so the number dipped. The scale measures how hard I push down on it, and then shows that push as kilograms.
items.why: A strong answer separates two things: how much of me there is, which stayed the same, and how hard I pushed, which changed.

items.p: Revathi stands still on a bathroom scale, holding a heavy bag at her waist. Then she lifts the bag high above her head and holds it there, still. Once she is still again, what does the scale show?
items.why: Wherever she holds the bag, its pull goes down through her arms and body into the scale. So once she is still, the number is the same. While she is lifting the bag, the number jumps up for a moment, because she pushes down to push the bag up. Many people guess 'less', because the bag is further from the scale.

items.p: Two forcemeters are hooked together and pulled. One reads 4 newtons. The other one reads ____ newtons.
items.why: Each forcemeter pulls on the other just as hard. Every pull comes with an equal pull back, so both always read the same.

items.p: Nila, a girl in Class 4, hooks her forcemeter to her uncle's and they pull. Nila says, 'My uncle is stronger, so his forcemeter will show more.' What is wrong with her idea?
opts: Nothing. The stronger person's forcemeter shows more
Both forcemeters always show the same, because each pull comes with an equal pull back
The weaker person's forcemeter shows more
Two forcemeters can't be hooked together
items.why: When the uncle pulls harder, the pull on Nila's side grows too, by exactly the same amount. Both forcemeters feel the one pull that passes through them. Being stronger lets him pull Nila along, but the readings stay equal.

items.p: When you made your rubber band forcemeter, you marked it by hanging 100 gram packets on it. Why not just draw the marks evenly with a ruler, without testing?
items.a: I did not know how far my rubber band stretches for each newton. Every band is different, and a band may not stretch evenly. Hanging packets I already knew put each mark exactly where that pull really is.
items.why: A strong answer says that the marks must come from known pulls. Putting marks on a tool using things you already know is called calibrating.

items.p: Match each thing to about how hard it pulls down on Earth.
pairs: about one tenth of a newton
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Every 100 grams pulls down with about 1 newton. So divide the grams by 100 to get the newtons. A 2 litre bottle holds about 2,000 grams of water, which is about 20 newtons.

items.p: Sort these tools. Does each one measure a force, or something else?
items.a: see items
items.why: A bathroom scale and a hanging spring balance both measure a push or a pull, then show it in kilograms. A ruler measures length, a jug measures how much water, and a thermometer measures how hot something is. The bathroom scale is the surprise for most people.

items.p: Meenakshi, her aunt and her friend Divya are arguing about what a bathroom scale measures.

views.says: The scale says kilograms. So it measures how much of me there is.
It measures how hard I push down on it. Then it turns that push into kilograms.
On the Moon the scale would show a smaller number. So it can't be measuring how much of me there is.

items.ask: Pick the person you agree with most. Use what happened in your bathroom scale test to back them up. Then say what the other side would answer back.
items.a: The aunt and Divya have the science right: the number dipped when you bent your knees, but no part of you went away. Meenakshi has a fair point too: on Earth, if you stand still, the push and the amount of you go together, so the kilogram number is useful. A strong answer uses the knee-bend result as evidence.
items.why: A strong answer names a side, uses a result from the test as evidence, and answers back fairly from another side. The best answers notice that everyone is partly right.

items.p: Draw your rubber band forcemeter with two marks on its card: 0 newtons and 1 newton. Draw what you hung on it to find where the 1 newton mark goes.
items.a: A rubber band hanging from the top of a card strip, with a paper clip hook at the bottom. A 0 mark is level with the hook when nothing hangs on it. A 1 newton mark is lower down, level with the hook when a 100 gram packet hangs on it.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the 0 mark made with nothing on the hook, and the 1 newton mark made with a known 100 gram packet.

items.p: In the Pull Detective test, Megha, a girl in Class 3, pulled open a drawer twice. Once she got 8 newtons, and once she got 12 newtons. What might have made the readings different? What should she do next?
items.a: She may have jerked the forcemeter once, or pulled it at a slant, or the drawer may have stuck. She should pull slowly and steadily, in a straight line, the same way each time. Then she should try three times and use the middle number.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real reason the readings could differ, and a way to make the test fairer. One try can be a fluke, which is why we repeat.

worksheets.context: This stretch worksheet uses the main ideas in new cases: zero mistakes, choosing a forcemeter, the Moon, the bathroom scale and your homemade forcemeter.

worksheets.title: From Molecules to the Moon (challenge)

items.p: Until 2019, one metal cylinder near Paris was the kilogram, by law. Imagine a speck of dust had landed on it. What would have happened to every other kilogram in the world?
items.a: By the rule of that time, the dusty cylinder was still exactly 1 kilogram. So the real kilogram would have grown a tiny bit, and every other kilogram weight in the world would have become a tiny bit too small.
items.why: A strong answer sees the strange problem: when a unit is one object, any change to the object changes the unit itself.

items.p: In 2019, scientists stopped using that metal cylinder, and fixed the kilogram using a number from nature, the Planck constant. Why?
opts: A number from nature does not change, but metal can slowly gain or lose tiny amounts
Metal is too expensive to keep
A number weighs less than a cylinder
items.why: The cylinder and its copies were slowly drifting apart by tiny amounts. As far as anyone can measure, the Planck constant is the same everywhere and never changes. So the kilogram, and the newton built on it, are now the same for everyone for ever.

items.p: In 1798, Henry Cavendish measured the gravity pull between lead balls. He watched his experiment through a telescope, from outside the room. Why do you think he did this?
items.a: So that he would not disturb it. Even the warmth of his body could stir the air and move the balls. The pull he was looking for was very tiny, so anything else could hide it.
items.why: A strong answer says that a tiny force is easily swamped, so everything else must be kept still. That is true of any very careful measurement.

items.p: Why couldn't Cavendish measure the pull between his lead balls with a spring forcemeter?
opts: The pull was far too tiny to stretch a spring enough to see
Springs had not been invented in 1798
Lead does not pull on anything
The balls were too big to hook on
items.why: The pull between his balls was much less than the weight of a grain of sand. A spring would not stretch a visible amount. So he hung the balls on a thin wire, which twists a little even for a tiny pull. Springs were known long before: Robert Hooke wrote about them in 1678.

items.p: Imagine a lift falling freely, with nothing slowing it down. Inside, a bag hangs from a forcemeter. What does the forcemeter show while the lift falls?
opts: Zero, because the bag and the forcemeter fall together
items.why: The bag and the forcemeter fall together at the same speed, so the bag does not pull on the spring at all. Gravity is still there, but nothing holds the bag back against it. Astronauts float for the same reason. Einstein used this idea to think about gravity in a new way.

items.p: Your homemade forcemeter showed 3 newtons for a pencil box. A kitchen scale said the box was 180 grams. Is your forcemeter right? Explain, and say what you would check.
items.a: Not quite. 180 grams pulls with about 1.8 newtons, which is nearly 2. My forcemeter showed 3, which is too big. I would check whether the pointer starts on zero, and test the marks again with a 100 gram packet.
items.why: A strong answer turns grams into newtons (divide by 100), compares the two, and suggests a real cause to check.

items.p: A shop's hanging spring balance shows 1 kilogram with nothing on its hook. A customer buys what the balance says is 3 kilograms of onions. How many kilograms of onions does she really get?
items.why: The balance starts at 1 instead of 0, so every reading is 1 kilogram too big. 3 take away 1 is 2 kilograms. The customer pays for 1 kilogram she never gets. That is why Legal Metrology officers check shop scales.

items.p: In the fair scale challenge, you used water to check whether a scale was honest. Why is water a good thing to check with?
items.a: One litre of water always has a mass of about 1 kilogram. Almost everybody can get water and measure a litre with a jug. Nobody owns it, so nobody can cheat with it.
items.why: A strong answer says the check is the same for everyone and nobody controls it. The gram was first defined in 1795 using water.

items.p: Design a forcemeter that could show the pull of a single sheet of paper. Draw it and label how it works.
items.a: For example, a long plastic ruler taped to the edge of a table, sticking out. The paper hangs from the far end, and a straw taped on as a pointer shows the bend against marks on a card.
items.why: A sheet of paper pulls with only about one twentieth of a newton. A strong design is sensitive: a tiny pull makes a big movement that is easy to see.

items.p: People often say 'about 10 newtons' for a 1 kilogram bag. Why do scientists say 'about', and not exactly 10?
opts: On Earth, the real number is about 9.8 newtons, and it changes a little from place to place
items.why: On Earth, 1 kilogram pulls down with about 9.8 newtons. It is a tiny bit more at the poles and a tiny bit less at the equator and on high mountains. 10 is close enough for everyday sums.

items.p: About 4,500 years ago, traders in the Indus Valley cities used stone weights in these sizes: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. The next weight in the set was ____.
items.why: Each weight is double the one before, and double 32 is 64. Picking 33 means the pattern was taken as adding 1. Shared weights let any buyer and seller in those cities agree on an amount.

items.p: In the story Ten Packets of Salt, a girl called Pushpa found that the contractor's balance was set wrongly. So who should check the scales in a market? Here are three views.

views.who: Selvi, who runs a vegetable shop in Madurai
views.says: I know my scale best. I check it myself every morning with a 1 kilogram weight.
The shopkeeper gains if the scale reads too high. Someone who gains should not be the only one who checks.
An officer should check every scale and put a seal on it. Then everyone trusts the same check.

items.ask: Pick the view you agree with most. Give a reason from the story or from your own scale checks. Then say one problem with your view that another person would point out.
items.a: Every view has a real point. Selvi checks often, but nobody checks her. Fathima is right about who gains, but customers cannot check every scale. An officer is fair to both sides, but visits only now and then. A strong answer might mix them: the officer seals the scale, and anyone may check it with a known weight.
items.why: A strong answer picks a side, uses evidence (for example, Pushpa's ten salt packets, or a scale that did not read zero), and names a fair weakness in its own view.

items.p: Scientists can measure gravity's pull very exactly. But what is gravity, deep down? Here are three answers.

views.says: Gravity is a pull between any two things. I can calculate it exactly, but I do not know how it reaches across empty space.
Gravity is not really a pull. Heavy things bend space and time around them, and other things follow the bends.
Gravity may be carried by tiny particles called gravitons. Nobody has found one yet.

items.ask: Which idea is easiest for you to picture? Say why. Then say what one of the others would answer back.
items.a: There is no settled answer, and scientists still argue. A strong answer notes what each idea has going for it. Newton's sums still work for bridges and rockets. Einstein's idea passed a famous test in 1919, when starlight was seen bending round the Sun. Gravitons have not been found.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason for its choice and fairly states another side. It can also say what would settle the question, such as finding a graviton.

items.p: One newton is the push that makes a 1 kilogram trolley speed up by 1 metre per second, every second. Now a 2 newton push acts on the same trolley, with nothing slowing it. What happens?
opts: It speeds up twice as fast
It moves at the same steady speed
It speeds up just as fast as with 1 newton
items.why: A force changes how a thing moves. Twice the push on the same thing gives twice the speeding up. Picking 'steady speed' is the old idea that a push only keeps things going. Newton showed that a push changes the speed.

items.p: Put these from the smallest force to the biggest: a small apple pulling on your hand, a feather pulling on your hand, the pull between the Earth and the Moon, a Saturn V rocket pushing off the ground.
items: a feather pulling on your hand
a small apple pulling on your hand
a Saturn V rocket pushing off the ground
the pull between the Earth and the Moon
items.a: order shown
items.why: A feather pulls with about one hundredth of a newton, and a small apple with about 1 newton. The Saturn V rocket pushed with about 34 million newtons. The Earth and the Moon pull on each other with about 200 million million million newtons. Most people guess the rocket is biggest, because a launch looks so huge.

items.p: A forcemeter that shows the same number every time you hang the same bag must be showing the right number.
items.why: False. A forcemeter whose pointer starts on 1 instead of 0 is wrong by the same amount every time. Giving the same answer again and again only shows it is steady. To know it is right, you must check it against something everyone trusts, like Pushpa's sealed salt packets.

worksheets.context: This challenge worksheet asks harder questions: how the kilogram is kept the same for everyone, how scientists measure very tiny and very huge forces, and who should check the scales.

quiz.p: Sneha, a girl in Class 3, invents a unit of pull called 'one eraser'. What must all her erasers be like?
opts: The same kind and size, so each one pulls the same
quiz.why: A unit only works if every one is the same size. Picking 'any erasers' means a big and a small eraser would count as the same, so her numbers would mean nothing.

quiz.p: Two careful children measure the same pull. One gets 5 and the other gets 20. They can both be right. How?
opts: One of them must have cheated
quiz.why: The same pull can be 5 big coins or 20 small coins. Picking 'cheated' means trusting the numbers without asking what each one counts.

quiz.p: A bridge builder in Chennai sends her numbers to a factory in Pune. Why must both of them use newtons?
opts: So the numbers mean the same thing in both places
Because Chennai is bigger than Pune
quiz.why: A shared unit means a pull written in Chennai is the same pull when it is read in Pune. Without it, the factory could make parts that are too weak.

quiz.p: Which of these pulls down on your hand with about 1 newton?
opts: A school bag full of books
quiz.why: A small apple of about 100 grams pulls with about 1 newton. A full school bag is more like 30 or 40 newtons. A feather is far less than 1 newton.

quiz.p: The newton is named after Isaac Newton. Who decided how big one newton is?
opts: People agreed on it together, using the kilogram, the metre and the second
Newton measured it inside an apple
quiz.why: The newton is an agreement between people. It was named in 1948, long after Newton died in 1727. Picking 'nature' mixes up the force, which is real, with the unit we count it in, which people chose.

quiz.p: Look at this forcemeter. Each small mark is half a newton. What is the reading?
quiz.why: The pointer is on the small mark between 7 and 8. Half a newton past 7 is 7 and a half newtons. Picking 7 or 8 means the small mark was not counted.

chart.title: A forcemeter. Each small mark is half a newton.

quiz.p: Ravi reads a forcemeter from far below, looking up at the pointer. What can go wrong?
opts: The pointer looks shifted, so he may read the wrong mark
quiz.why: Looking from below or above makes the pointer seem to sit on a different mark. Reading with your eyes level with the pointer gives the true reading.

quiz.p: Why does a forcemeter use a spring, and not a stiff steel rod?
opts: A spring stretches more for a bigger pull, so the pointer can show the size
A rod would be too heavy
quiz.why: The stretch is what shows the size of the pull. A stiff rod would hardly stretch at all, so the pointer would not move.

quiz.p: A spring stretches 2 centimetres when it is pulled with 1 newton. How far does it stretch for 3 newtons, inside its range?
quiz.why: Each newton adds about 2 centimetres, so 3 newtons give 3 times 2, which is 6 centimetres. Robert Hooke found this rule in 1678. Picking 3 means the newtons were read as centimetres.

quiz.p: Before the coin test, you guessed how many coins you would need, and said why. Why say a reason, not just a number?
opts: So after the test you can see whether your reason was right
To make the test take longer
Because a reason changes the result
quiz.why: A guess with a reason can be checked. If the result surprises you, your reason was wrong somewhere, and you learn what to think again.

quiz.p: Pooja tests two notebooks. She slides the thin one on a smooth table, and the thick one on a rough mat. What is unfair about her test?
opts: She changed two things at once, so she can't tell which one made the difference
quiz.why: In a fair test, you change only one thing. Pooja changed the notebook and the surface, so if the numbers differ, she can't say why.

quiz.p: A packet of rice is taken from the Earth to the Moon. What stays the same?
opts: The amount of rice in it, its mass
quiz.why: The mass stays the same, because no rice is added or taken away. The pull, its weight, is about one sixth on the Moon. Picking 'how hard it pulls' mixes up mass and weight.

quiz.p: On the Moon, a bathroom scale shows a 30 kilogram girl as about 5 kilograms. Did she lose 25 kilograms of her body?
opts: No. The scale shows her push, and the Moon pulls her less
Yes, the Moon makes people smaller
quiz.why: A bathroom scale measures how hard you push down on it. The Moon pulls about one sixth as hard, so she pushes about one sixth as hard. All of her is still there.

quiz.p: You press your palm on a table. Deep down, what pushes your hand back?
opts: The electrons in the table push away the electrons in your hand
quiz.why: Electrons push other electrons away. So your hand and the table push apart, and that push is what you feel. Picking 'tiny springs' is a fair picture, but the real spring is the electric push between atoms.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still not know?
opts: What gravity really is, deep down
How to measure a pull in newtons
Whether a spring stretches when it is pulled
quiz.why: Measuring forces is well understood. What gravity is, deep down, is still an open question. Newton, Einstein and physicists today give different answers.

open_questions.q: What is a force, really, deep down?
open_questions.why_open: Newton could describe gravity but not explain it. Einstein said gravity is bent space and time. Particle physicists think forces are carried by particles. Nobody has joined these into one picture.

open_questions.q: Does a graviton, a particle that carries gravity, exist?
open_questions.why_open: Many physicists think it should. It would be so hard to catch that nobody knows how to build an experiment to find one.

open_questions.q: Why do measurements of gravity's strength disagree?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have measured the strength of gravity, often called big G, many times since Cavendish. The best results still disagree more than they should. Nobody is sure why.

open_questions.q: How small a force can we ever measure?
open_questions.why_open: Quantum physics says measuring always nudges things a little. Clever new tools can get around some limits. Nobody knows how far this can go.

open_questions.q: Exactly why does a small box feel heavier than a big box of the same weight?
open_questions.why_open: The size-weight illusion was described in 1891. Scientists still argue about how much comes from what we expect, and how much from how we grip and lift.

open_questions.q: How do millions of tiny molecular pulls work together to make a muscle strong and smooth?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can find one molecule's pull. How so many of them work together so well is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Is the strength of gravity the same everywhere in the universe, and at every time?
open_questions.why_open: As far as we can tell, yes. But scientists keep testing it. If it changed even a little, our ideas about the universe would have to change.

open_questions.q: Why does the pull needed to slide something grow so evenly with its weight?
open_questions.why_open: Leonardo da Vinci noticed this rule around 1500, and Guillaume Amontons wrote it down in 1699. It works well. But why it works, at the size of atoms, is still being studied. It seems to depend on how many tiny bumps really touch.

maths.problem: Look at the forcemeter in the picture. The big numbers are whole newtons. Each small mark between them is half a newton. What is the reading?
maths.explain: The pointer is past the 3, but before the 4. It sits on the small mark halfway between them. Each small mark is half a newton. So the reading is 3 newtons and half a newton more. That is 3 and a half newtons.
maths.why_maths: Every forcemeter has a scale, and counting the gaps between its numbers is how you read it truly.

maths.problem: In the coin-pull investigation, Meera, a girl in Class 3, needed 6 five-rupee coins to start her notebook sliding. Her grandmother tested the same notebook with one-rupee coins and needed 12. On a ruler balance, one five-rupee coin balanced two one-rupee coins. Did they find the same pull, or different pulls?
maths.answer: The same pull. 6 five-rupee coins pull as hard as 12 one-rupee coins.
maths.explain: One five-rupee coin pulls as hard as 2 one-rupee coins. So 6 five-rupee coins pull as hard as 6 lots of 2 one-rupee coins. 6 times 2 is 12. Meera's grandmother needed 12. The numbers were different, but the pull was the same. Only the unit was different.
maths.why_maths: Two numbers can only be compared in the same unit. Multiplying turns one unit into the other, the way you change rupees into paise.
maths.context: In the coin-pull investigation, you dropped coins into a hanging cup until a notebook started to slide. These numbers are made up.

maths.problem: Here are made-up results from the coin-pull investigation. One notebook needed 6 coins. Two stacked notebooks needed 12. Three needed 17. Spot the pattern. About how many coins would four notebooks need? Why?
maths.answer: About 23 coins, because each extra notebook needs about 6 more coins.
maths.explain: From 1 notebook to 2, the coins went up by 6. From 2 to 3, they went up by 5. So each notebook adds about 5 or 6 coins. 17 add 6 is 23. Real results are never perfectly even, so 22, 23 or 24 are all good predictions. If you have a fourth notebook, test your prediction.
maths.why_maths: Spotting how the numbers grow lets you predict a test before you do it. Then you can check whether you were right.
maths.context: In the coin-pull investigation, you counted the coins it took to start one, two and three stacked notebooks sliding.

maths.problem: In the story Ten Packets of Salt, Mohan Lal's balance was set wrongly. Ten 1 kilogram packets of salt showed as only 5 kilograms. Basanti's basket showed 14 kilograms on the same balance. Something is odd. What was going wrong, and how heavy was the basket really?
maths.answer: The balance showed 5 kilograms too little every time. The basket was really 19 kilograms.
maths.explain: The ten packets were agreed to be 10 kilograms, but the balance said 5. So it was 5 kilograms short. Its pointer started in the wrong place, so every reading was short by the same 5. To fix a reading, add 5 back. 14 add 5 is 19. That is exactly what the balance showed once the zero was fixed.
maths.why_maths: When a scale's zero is wrong, every reading is out by the same amount. Finding that amount once, with something everyone agrees on, fixes every reading.
maths.context: In the story Ten Packets of Salt, Pushpa tested a spring balance with ten 1 kilogram packets. In the fair scale challenge, you checked a scale in the same way, with water.

maths.problem: In the forcemeter tug of war, Ayesha, a girl in Class 3, pulled against her father. Ayesha's forcemeter showed 5 newtons, and her father's showed 5 newtons too. Her father said, 'So together we are pulling with 10 newtons.' Is he right? Explain.
maths.answer: No. The pull through the two forcemeters is 5 newtons. Each forcemeter shows the same pull, seen from its own end.
maths.explain: Ayesha pulls on her father with 5 newtons, and he pulls back on her with 5 newtons. Both forcemeters feel that one pull passing through them. Adding 5 and 5 counts the same pull twice. If he let go, both forcemeters would drop to 0 together.
maths.why_maths: Adding only makes sense when the numbers count different things. Asking 'what does each number count?' stops you adding the same thing twice.
maths.context: In the forcemeter tug of war, two people hook two forcemeters together and pull. They read both forcemeters.

maths.problem: In the Moon tiffin activity, your 600 gram tiffin pulled with about 6 newtons on Earth. The Moon pulls about one sixth as hard. Predict: about how hard would the same tiffin pull on the Moon?
maths.explain: One sixth means sharing into 6 equal parts and taking one part. 6 newtons shared into 6 parts is 1 newton each. So on the Moon the tiffin pulls with about 1 newton, like a small apple on Earth.
maths.why_maths: Sharing a force into equal parts shows how much weaker the Moon's pull is than the Earth's.
maths.context: In the Moon tiffin activity, you poured out rice to feel how light your lunch would be on the Moon.

maths.problem: In the pull detective experiment, these were the biggest readings. Slipper 2 newtons, drawer 5 newtons, cupboard door 6 newtons, chair 15 newtons, fridge door 18 newtons, school bag 25 newtons. Draw a bar chart. How much bigger is the fridge door's pull than the drawer's?
maths.answer: The fridge door's pull is 13 newtons bigger. Here is the bar chart.
maths.explain: Draw one bar for each pull, as tall as its reading. Then compare the fridge door and the drawer. 18 take away 5 is 13. So the fridge door needs 13 newtons more.
maths.why_maths: After the pull detective test you have six numbers. A bar chart shows the biggest and smallest pulls at a glance.

how_we_found_out.who: French scientists in 1795, and the countries that share the kilogram
how_we_found_out.story: For most of history, every town had its own weights. A ser in one market was not a ser in the next. So people often argued about how much they had bought. In 1795, France made a new rule. A gram would be the mass of a tiny cube of water, 1 centimetre on each side. Water is the same everywhere, so anyone could check it. In 1889, many countries agreed to share one kilogram. It was a metal cylinder, kept locked near Paris. Each country got a copy. India's copy is in New Delhi. People thought the metal would never change. But years later, the copies were weighed against it again. They no longer matched exactly. So in 2019, scientists stopped using the metal cylinder. Now the kilogram is set by a fixed number from physics. Anyone with the right machine can check it, anywhere in the world.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed one guarded lump of metal would stay exactly the same for ever. When the copies were checked years later, they had drifted apart by a tiny amount.

roots.context: We have been inventing units of pull, counting coins and water, and meeting the newton. Now we ask what a number like '5 newtons' really is, and what that says about us and the world.

deep_truth.truth: One notebook needed 6 big coins to start sliding, or 12 small coins. The pull was the same, so the number changed only because the coin changed. A number for a force tells you how many units fit, so it depends on the unit people choose. That is why it is useful only when everyone counts in one agreed unit, like the newton.
deep_truth.habit: We usually think a number like 12 tells us how big a pull is. In fact a number only says how many units fit, so it means nothing without its unit.
deep_truth.evidence: In the coin-pull test, a child and a grown-up counted different numbers of coins for the same notebook. Both counts were right, because they used different coins as their unit.

three.who_am_i: Your hand can feel that one pull is bigger than another. To tell someone else exactly how big it is, you both need to share one unit.
three.what_is_life: A crow feels the push of the wind, and a root senses which way is down, without any numbers. People invented numbers for forces so they could share and compare what they sense.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth pulled mangoes down long before anyone had a unit for force. The pull is part of nature. The number in newtons is something people added, by agreeing on a unit.

roots.thread: Before anyone measured it, the notebook's pull was just a pull, with no number. To count it, people choose one small pull as the unit, such as one coin, one ratti seed or one newton. Then they count how many of that one unit fit. Every number in newtons, from a molecule's tug to the pull between the Earth and the Moon, counts that same one unit. Because everyone starts from the same one, a number in Madurai can be compared with a number in Paris.

teachings.teaching: Truth is one. The wise call it by many names.
teachings.link: One notebook's pull was counted as 6 big coins, 12 small coins or about half a newton. The numbers changed with the unit. The pull itself stayed the same.

teachings.teaching: The heavens were raised, and a balance was set. So do not cheat the balance. Weigh fairly, and do not make the balance short.
teachings.link: A balance is a promise between people. In the story Ten Packets of Salt, one wrong pointer cheated every porter, until a shared standard showed it.

science.text: Since 20 May 2019, the kilogram, and so the newton, is fixed by the Planck constant, a constant of nature. People still chose the exact number it is given, so the new kilogram matched the old one. A Kibble balance can turn that number into a real kilogram anywhere.

Units are clearly chosen by people. Philosophers of science still argue about the laws of nature. Are they simply found in nature, or partly shaped by the way people choose to describe and count things?

other_view.who: Protagoras, a Greek thinker of about 2,400 years ago, as Plato reports in the Theaetetus
other_view.view: Protagoras said that each person is the measure of all things. What feels heavy to you is heavy for you. On this view, the feeling in your own hand is the truest measure. A shared unit leaves out how differently each of us feels the same load.

practice.title: How many coins can your hand count?
practice.say: Close your eyes and hold out one open hand, palm up. I will put coins on it, one at a time, very gently. Say 'now' each time you feel your hand get heavier. Breathe slowly while you wait. Open your eyes. Did you feel every coin, or did some go unnoticed? Your hand felt the weight, but could it count it? What would it need?
